bib.title: Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents", Asaf Yehudai, Lilach Eden, Alan Li, Guy Uziel, Yilun Zhao, Roy Bar-Haim, Arman Cohan, Michal Shmueli-Scheuer. No venue is printed; the only stamp is "arXiv:2503.16416v2 [cs.AI] 23 Apr 2026", so cite it as a preprint, v2 (2026-04), first posted 2025-03.
First-author affiliations as printed: Asaf Yehudai, "1The Hebrew University of Jerusalem 2IBM Research". Other authors are IBM Research and Yale University.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/yehudai-2025-survey-evaluation-llm-based-agents.pdf

COVERAGE: 25 of 25 pages, 115,665 chars.
- Read in full: body pp.1-9, Limitations p.10, appendices A-E pp.20-25, and the references on pp.10-13 and 18-19.
- Not read line by line: the references on pp.14-17 (about 17k chars). I keyword-scanned them for embedded instructions and read only the last part.
- Figure captions were extracted. There are two figures, both taxonomy trees.

DOES IT CONTRIBUTE ANYTHING OF ITS OWN? Mostly not. It runs no experiments, and every performance number is second-hand. Its own contributions are organisational:
- a five-part taxonomy;
- Table 1 (p.6), which codes 8 benchmarks on data, environment, interface, metric and safety;
- Table 2 (p.8), a feature matrix of 8 eval frameworks;
- the gap list in §7.2;
- the benchmark recommendations in Appendix E.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: What to evaluate splits into capabilities (planning, tool use, self-reflection, memory), application-specific agents (web, SWE, scientific, conversational), generalist agents, and developer frameworks, plus cross-cutting benchmark dimensions.
  number: none
  setup: the authors' taxonomy
  quote: "(1) Core LLM capabilities needed for agentic workflows, like planning, and tool use; (2) Application-specific benchmarks such as web and SWE agents; (3) Evaluation of generalist agents; (4) Analysis of agent benchmarks' core dimensions; and (5) Evaluation frameworks and tools for agent developers."
  where: p.1 abstract
- claim: Binary outcome metrics do not show intermediate progress; the survey calls for standardised trajectory-level metrics.
  number: none
  setup: authors' judgement, no measurement
  quote: "Many current benchmarks rely on coarse-grained, end-to-end success metrics that, while useful for gauging overall performance, fall short in diagnosing specific agent failures."
  where: p.9 §7.2 (also p.6 Metric)
- claim: Frameworks grade at three granularities: final response, stepwise, and trajectory. Trajectory grading is either reference-based (exact, partial, unordered, subset matching) or reference-free (LLM judge).
  number: none
  setup: vendor documentation for LangSmith, Vertex AI and AgentEvals; in Table 2 only 3 of 8 frameworks are ticked for trajectory assessment
  quote: "reference-based methods are inherently limited, as multiple valid paths typically exist and manual reference specification is often infeasible."
  where: p.7 §6
- claim: Stepwise judging assumes steps are independent.
  number: none
  setup: authors' judgement; they cite Galileo's "action advancement" metric as the counter-example
  quote: "These approaches assume that each action can be meaningfully assessed in isolation, overlooking dependencies between steps."
  where: p.7
- claim: Cost is a gap in two ways: benchmarks ignore the agent's cost, and frameworks ignore the cost of running the evaluation.
  number: none
  setup: authors' judgement; the agent-cost point is credited to Kapoor et al. (2024b)
  quote: "current frameworks overlook the cost incurred by the evaluation process itself, specifically when scaling over a large number of traces with expensive LLM judges."
  where: p.8; the agent-cost gap is on p.9
- claim: Robustness is measured by pass^k; safety and policy compliance are rarely tested.
  number: 1 of the 8 benchmarks in Table 1 (TAU-Bench) is marked "Yes" for safety
  setup: the authors' own coding of 8 benchmarks
  quote: "Robustness is often quantified via pass^k, the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds across all k independent runs."
  where: p.6
- claim: Static environments miss compounding errors.
  number: none
  setup: e.g. the original Mind2Web
  quote: "incorrect actions have no downstream consequences, missing compounding failures that can ultimately cause task failure."
  where: p.6
- claim: Benchmarks conflate the backbone LLM with the harness; the survey asks for protocols that vary each independently.
  number: none
  setup: authors' judgement; they cite Harbor and Exgentic as first steps
  quote: "Most current agent benchmarks conflate two distinct evaluation targets"
  where: p.9
- claim: Second-hand benchmark sizes and scores, none re-measured by the survey.
  - SWE-bench Verified: "a high-quality subset of 500 samples" (p.4).
  - SWE-Lancer: "1,400 freelance tasks from Upwork with total payouts over $1M" (p.4).
  - SWE-bench Pro: "1,865 human-verified tasks spanning 41 repositories ... Model performance remains below 25% Pass@1" (p.4).
  - Mind2Web 2 (Gou et al. 2025): "agents achieve 50−70% of human performance" (p.24).
  - Leaderboard snapshots with no model or source named:
    - WebArena: "as of April 19, 2026, top performance has reached 74.3%" (pp.24-25).
    - SWE-bench Verified: "approximately 80%" (p.25).
    - SWE-bench Pro: "hovers around 46%" (p.25).

LIMITS
- Conceded by the authors (p.10): the survey is a snapshot, the selection is representative rather than exhaustive, per-benchmark depth is shallow, and the gap list is "foresight and interpretation".
- Not stated by the authors:
  - There is no count of papers screened and no PRISMA-style flow. Appendix A describes keyword search, snowballing and expert consultation without numbers.
  - The gaps are asserted, not quantified. For example, no share of benchmarks reporting cost is given.
  - Table 2 is coded from vendor material, and the caption admits "some of these capabilities are still in initial phases of development".
  - The paper contradicts itself on SWE-bench Pro: "below 25% Pass@1" on p.4 against "around 46%" on p.25.
  - The author group is IBM-heavy, and the works it cites as steps toward solutions (Exgentic/Bandel et al. 2026a,b) are the authors' own.
  - The leaderboard figures will date quickly.

BUILDS ON
- Wang et al. (2024a), survey of LLM-based autonomous agents.
- Kapoor et al. (2024b), "AI agents that matter", for cost.
- Zhu et al. (2025), best practices for agentic benchmarks.
- Zhuge et al. (2024), Agent-as-a-Judge.
- Yao et al. (2024), τ-Bench, for pass^k.
- Brockman et al. (2016), OpenAI Gym.

CODE: none.

FIGURES: one candidate, Figure 1, p.2, "Overview of the paper with core works." It is a taxonomy tree mapping each evaluation target to its named benchmarks, and it shows the capability / application / generalist / framework split at a glance. Figure 2 (p.21) is the fuller version of the same tree. Table 1 (p.6) is arguably more useful for the note, but it is a table and is easy to retype.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions were found.
- The extraction is clean apart from dropped spaces after bold run-in heads (e.g. "Memorymechanisms") and "WebV oyager".
- The mapped note does not currently list arXiv 2503.16416 in its sources.
